title: The second jhana
hook: a lake fed by a spring from within (MN 39)

segments.voice: Yesterday: jhana, and your line, soaked through. Did one good moment get three whole breaths to soak in? Day three hundred ninety-seven.

Some lakes are filled by rivers: water pours down from the hills, and if the rivers dry up, the lake shrinks. Some are topped up by rain. And some, the rare ones, are filled from beneath. A cold spring wells up from the lakebed, and the lake stays full even in a dry season. You can't see where the water is coming from. It just keeps arriving. Today: the second jhana, and the inner spring.
screen: `FED BY RIVERS.` → `FED BY RAIN.` → `FED FROM BENEATH.`

segments.voice: In MN 39 the Buddha describes the next stage. With the stilling of directed and sustained thought, a person enters the second jhana: inner stillness, the mind become one, without directed or sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration. Then his picture. A lake whose waters well up from below. No stream flows in from the east, the west, the north or the south. The sky doesn't fill it with rain from time to time. But a cool spring wells up within it and soaks the whole lake, so that no part of it is left untouched. Set it beside yesterday's picture. In the first jhana, water had to be added by a hand, sprinkled and kneaded into the powder. The joy was born of seclusion, of stepping away. Here the hand is gone. Thinking has gone quiet. And the joy is born of concentration itself; it rises from inside. Two Pali words carry this. Sampasadana: inner clearness, or inner confidence, like muddy water settling until you can see the bottom. And ekodibhava: the mind becoming single, unified. The calm doesn't depend on anything outside: no good news, no compliment, no perfect weather. The texts give this stage a lovely name, too. In SN 21.1, Moggallana is taught that the second jhana is what's called noble silence. Not the silence of a closed mouth, but of a mind that has stopped talking to itself.
screen: `THINKING GROWS STILL.` · `A LAKE FED FROM WITHIN.` · `NO RIVER, NO RAIN.` · `NOBLE SILENCE.` · then, large: `THE INNER SPRING.`

segments.voice: Don't go looking for calm out there. Sit, let the breath settle, and when a thought comes, let it pass without picking it up. Between thoughts there may be small gaps: a breath or two with nothing to do. Rest in one of those gaps, and notice whether anything wells up on its own: quiet, coolness, a little gladness. If nothing does, the gap itself is enough. The bell holds the time.
The second jhana. Thinking grows still, and joy wells up from within, like a lake fed by its own spring.
Your line: the inner spring. Today, when you reach for something outside to feel better, pause for one breath and check whether something quieter is already there. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Meditators who train in the jhanas usually do so under a teacher's guidance, often on retreat; many Buddhists also use the phrase 'noble silence' for periods of silence kept at retreats.

pairs: a lake fed by a spring
a name for the second jhana

myth: in the second jhana, directed and sustained thought go still
that stilling is what marks the move from the first.
the lake in the simile is kept full by rain
no stream, no rain: a cool spring wells up from within.
by the second jhana, the joy is gone
joy and pleasure remain, now born of concentration.

fork.setup: a lake has no streams flowing in and gets no rain. how does it stay full, in the Buddha's simile?
options: it doesn't; it slowly dries up
a cool spring wells up from within it
fork.reveal: the spring rises from inside and soaks the whole lake. the calm of the second jhana needs nothing poured in from outside.

original.note: Pali sampasādana: inner clearness or confidence, like water settling clear; a quality of the second jhāna.

trapdoor: what you thought: a deeper level of the same thing.
what it means: thinking grows still, and calm and joy rise from within, needing nothing added.
what a scholar hears: sampasādana can mean both inner clarity and inner confidence; in SN 21.1 the second jhāna is called ariya tuṇhībhāva, noble silence.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the spring-fed lake)

notes: SN 21.1: Moggallana (Kolita) reports being taught that the second jhana is called noble silence (ariya tunhibhava); please confirm.
The two senses of sampasadana (clarity / confidence) and the 'muddy water settling' image are interpretive; please confirm they fit.
Simile details (no inflow from four directions, no rain) retold from MN 39 from memory.
